Tabāraka (تبارك) is a verb derived from barakah (blessing; abundance of good). It is also said to mean "He has become exalted," and it is specific to God Most High; no present-tense form (muḍāriʿ) has been pronounced for it. ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾: meaning the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and of this world and the Hereafter. It is also said: meaning the sovereignty of kings in this world, as in His saying, "Owner of the Kingdom" (Mālik al-Mulk). The first meaning is more general and more magnificent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 2:

﴿He created death and life﴾. That is, the death and life of creatures. It has also been said: death refers to this world, because its inhabitants die, and life refers to the Hereafter, because it is everlasting. This is like His saying: ﴿And indeed, the Last Abode – that is the true life﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64]. On this view, it is a description by means of the verbal noun (wasf bil-masdar), though the first interpretation is more apparent. ﴿That He may test you﴾, meaning, that He may examine you. God's testing of His servants is only so that the proof may be established against them by what proceeds from them, though God had already known what they would do before it occurred. The meaning is: that He may test you and then recompense you for what has become manifest from you. ﴿Which of you is best in deed﴾. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it and then said: "Which of you is best in deed, and most fearful of God, and most scrupulous in abstaining from what God has forbidden, and quickest in obedience to God."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verses 3–4:

﴿Seven heavens, layered one above another﴾. That is, some of them above others. Ṭibāq (layered) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an attribute of the heavens, or it stands for an elided modifier, the sense being "possessing layers." It has also been said that it is the plural of ṭabaqah (layer).

﴿You will see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾. That is: no lack of proportion and no departure from perfection. The meaning is that the creation of the heavens is in the utmost perfection. It has also been said that He intends the creation of all created things, and there is no doubt that all created things are perfect. However, restricting the verse to the creation of the heavens is more evident, since it comes after His saying ﴿He created seven heavens, layered one above another﴾. So His saying ﴿You will see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾ clarifies and completes what precedes it.

The address in His saying ﴿You will see﴾, and in what follows, ﴿So return the gaze﴾, is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to every addressee so that he may take heed. ﴿Then return the gaze, do you see any rifts?﴾ Fuṭūr (rifts) means cracks, plural of fiṭr, which is a split. Irjā' al-baṣar (returning the gaze) means repeating the looking. The meaning of the verse is a command to look at the sky, and one will see in it no cracks or flaws; rather, it is joined together and level.

﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾, that is, look again and again, for verification and certainty. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of the dual in "twice" (kartayn) is multiplicity, not two specifically, like their saying labbayka, whose meaning is many responses.

﴿Your gaze will return to you dazzled, while it is weary﴾. Khāsi' (dazzled) is one who has been kept away from the thing he sought, and ḥasīr (weary) is one who is exhausted and overtaken by fatigue. The meaning of the verse is that when you look at the sky again and again to see in it cracks or flaws, your gaze returns and sees nothing of that. It is as if it were dazzled, because it did not obtain what it sought of seeing cracks and flaws, and it is at the same time weary from the intensity of looking and the abundance of contemplation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 5:

﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾. The nearest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya) is the one closest to us. The lamps (al-masabih) are intended to mean the stars. If all the stars are in the nearest heaven, there is no difficulty, since they are visible to us from it. It is also possible that He means He adorned the nearest heaven with the stars that are in it, to the exclusion of those in other heavens. Moreover, the statement about the location of the planets and which heaven they are in has not been reported in the Revealed Law (al-shari'a). ﴿And We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾. That is, We made from them missiles, since the fixed stars do not pelt the devils. It is like your saying, "I honoured the sons of so-and-so," when you honoured some of them. The word rujum (missiles) is the plural of rajm, which is a verbal noun (masdar) used to name that by which one pelts. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of the stars being missiles against the devils is that shooting stars (shuhub) break off from the stars to pelt the devils who eavesdrop on the heaven. So the pelting shooting stars are detached from the fire of the planets, and it is not that the pelting objects are the planets themselves, since they are fixed in the sphere. Qatada said: God created the stars for three things: as an adornment of the heaven, as missiles against the devils, and as guidance by which one is guided in the darknesses of land and sea. ﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾. That is, for the devils.

They heard for it a braying (shahiq), the most hideous sound a donkey makes. What is meant here is the sound heard from Hell because of the intensity of its boiling and its terror, or the braying of its inhabitants; the first is more apparent. "And it boils over" means it seethes with its inhabitants like the seething of a cooking pot with what is in it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 8–9:

﴿It is about to burst apart from [its] fury﴾ That is, Hell is about to split apart, some of it from the rest, because of its intense rage against the disbelievers. It may be that it is itself enraged, and it may be that the intended meaning is the rage of the guardians (al-zabaniyah). The first is more apparent, because the state of the guardians is mentioned after this. The rage of the Fire may be literal, through a perception that God creates for it, or it may be an expression of its intensity. ﴿Every time a group is thrown into it﴾ That is, every time a company of the disbelievers is cast into Hell, the guardians ask them: ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ That is, no messenger. This question is posed in the manner of rebuke and the establishment of proof against them, and for this reason they confessed and said: ﴿Yes, indeed, a warner did come to us﴾. His saying "every time" requires that this be said of every group that is cast into the Fire. ﴿You are only in great error﴾ may be the words of the angels to the disbelievers, or the words of the disbelievers to the messengers in the world.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verses 10–11:

﴿And they will say﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers. That is, ﴿"Had we been listening"﴾ to the words of the messengers and reasoning soundly, ﴿"we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze."﴾

﴿So they will acknowledge their sin﴾: their acknowledgment at this point is of no benefit to them, since it comes at a time when acknowledgment does not profit them. Their sin here is intended to mean their denial of the messengers.

﴿So away with the companions of the Blaze!﴾: fasuhqan (away with) is in the accusative by an implied verb, in the sense of a supplication against them.

﴿بِٱلْغَيْبِ﴾ (in the unseen): there are two opinions. The first is that it means they are absent from people, unseen by them, and so this describes them as sincere. The second is that "the unseen" is what is hidden from them of the matters of the Hereafter and other things. This second view, however, only fits well in His words: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

﴿وَأَسِرُّواْ قَوْلَكُمْ أَوِ ٱجْهَرُواْ بِهِ﴾ (And keep your speech secret or speak aloud): the meaning is that whether you speak aloud or keep it secret, indeed God knows both the open and the secret.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 14:

﴿Should He not know, He who created?﴾ This is a proof that God, exalted is He, knows everything, because the Creator knows what He has created. It is possible that ﴿man khalaqa﴾ ("He who created") is the subject, meaning the Creator, and the object is omitted, its implied sense being: "Should the Creator not know His creation?" Or ﴿man khalaqa﴾ may be the object, with an implied subject, its sense being: "Should God not know whom He created?" The first is more preferred, because "man khalaqa" when it is the object is restricted to those who have reason, whereas the first meaning encompasses both those who have reason and those who do not.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 15:**

﴿The earth made subservient (dhalulan)﴾ Fa'ul here is used in the sense of maf'ul: meaning madhulah (tamed, subdued), so it is like a riding animal and a milking animal. ﴿So walk in its shoulders (manakibiha)﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: these are the mountains. It was also said: the sides and the regions. It was also said: the roads. The meaning is an enumeration of the blessing in making walking on the earth easy, and he metaphorically attributed to it subjugation (adh-dhull) and "shoulders" (al-manakib), by way of likening it to beasts. ﴿And to Him is the resurrection (al-nushur)﴾ meaning: the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verses 16–17:

﴿Are you secure that He who is in the heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you, and then it sways?﴾ The purpose of this verse is threat and warning to the disbelievers. Likewise the verse after it, ﴿Or are you secure that He who is in the heaven will not send against you a violent wind (ḥāṣib), so you will know how My warning (nadhīr) was?﴾ The word ﴿تَمُورُ﴾ (tamūru, "sways violently") is mentioned in Surah al-Ṭūr [9]: ﴿the day the sky will sway violently﴾. The word ﴿حَاصِباً﴾ (ḥāṣiban) may mean stones or a violent wind. The word ﴿نَذِيرِ﴾ (nadhīr) carries the meaning of warning (indhār), and likewise the word al-nakīr carries the meaning of denunciation (inkār).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 19:

﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them in?﴾ This is a reminder to reflect on the flight of birds through the air without anything holding them up. Ṣāffāt (spreading out) is the plural of ṣāffa, which is the bird that extends its wings for flight. Al-qabḍ (folding in) means drawing the two wings in against the sides. The verb yaqbiḍna (folding in) is coordinated with ṣāffāt (spreading out), because the verb here carries the sense of a noun, its implied form being qābiḍāt (folding in). If it is asked: why was it not said qābiḍāt in the same pattern as ṣāffāt? The answer is that spreading the wings is the basic state of flight, just as extending the limbs is the basic state of swimming, so it was expressed with the active participle form, for its continuity and frequency. As for folding the wings, the bird does it only occasionally, for rest and for support, so it was expressed with the verbal form, for its infrequency.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verses 20–21:

﴿Who is it that is an army for you to support you, other than the Most Merciful?﴾ This is an address to the disbelievers, in the manner of rebuke, threat, and establishing the proof against them. The particle ﴿amm﴾ (an interrogative particle, here meaning denial directed at ﴿man﴾) entered upon ﴿man﴾ and was assimilated into it. Likewise ﴿Who is it that provides for you?﴾ The pronoun in ﴿amsak﴾ refers to Allah, meaning: who would provide for you if Allah withholds His provision? ﴿Rather, they persisted﴾, meaning they continued in obstinate rebellion and aversion from faith.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 22:

﴿Is then one who walks prone on his face﴾ — the verse is a question posing the two states, asking which of them is better guided. Its purpose is to rebuke the disbelievers. There are two opinions regarding its meaning. The first: walking here is a metaphor for pursuing the path of guidance or misguidance in this world. The second: it is literal, referring to walking in the Hereafter, because the disbeliever will be driven to walk on his face toward Hell.

As for the first opinion, it has been said that the one who walks prone is Abu Jahl, and the one who walks upright is our master Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that the upright one is Hamzah. And it has been said that the verse is general, applying to every believer and every disbeliever. These opinions can also apply to the second meaning.

The word mukib (مُكِبّ) refers to one who falls on his face. It is said: akabba al-rajulu (أكبّ الرجل), and kabbahu ghayruhu (كبّه غيره). The transitive form is without the hamzah, and the intransitive form takes the hamzah, unlike other verbs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 25:

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ The pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and the promise is meant to be either the Resurrection (al-ba'th) or their punishment in this world.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 27:

﴿When they see it approaching﴾: the subject of the verb (the pronoun in "they saw it") refers to the disbelievers, and the object pronoun refers to the punishment contained in the promise. ﴿Drawing near﴾: that is, close at hand. It is also said: visibly before them. ﴿The faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾: that is, evil will appear in them because of what has befallen them. ﴿And it will be said: "This is what you used to call for"﴾: "tadda'una" is from the form "tafta'ila" (ta-fa'-'a-la) from "du'a'" (calling), meaning you were asking for it and seeking it hastily. Those who say this are the angels, or it is said to them through the tongue of the situation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 67, verse 28:

﴿Say, "Have you considered: if Allah should destroy me and those with me, or have mercy on us, then who would protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"﴾ The occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers used to wish for the destruction of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. So Allah commanded him to say to them: "If Allah destroys me and those who are with me, or shows us mercy, you will still not be saved from the painful punishment in any case." The word "destruction" (al-halak) here may be understood to mean death or something other than death. The meaning of ﴿who would protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment﴾ is: who would prevent them from the punishment?

Qur'an 67:30 says: ﴿Say: "Have you considered: if your water should sink away into the earth, who would bring you flowing water?"﴾ The verse is an argument against the polytheists. "Ghawr" (sinking, deep withdrawal) is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description, so it carries the sense of "ghayir," meaning going away into the earth. "Mu'in" means abundant, flowing water. Scholars differed over its pattern: is it the form "fa'il" or "maf'ul"? The meaning is: if your water that you drink sinks away, will anyone other than God bring you water that flows?
